sentences.text: The only known individual was a small dryosaurid estimated at 1.6 meters in length, comparable to immature Dryosaurus and Dysalotosaurus.

The foot is unique among ornithopods because the first digit (hallux — the backward-pointing toe) includes only a single phalanx bone, whereas most basal ornithopods had two and most derived ones lost it entirely.
The foot claw formula is 1-3-4-5-0, with the first toe claw being extremely reduced, flattened vertically, elongated, and pointed.
The species name nanohallucis means "small hallux," referring to the small size of the big toe.
This represents a case of parallel evolution where a foot digit was lost from the first toe, leaving a very small, bone-tip-like remnant.
In 1999, an amateur paleontologist found the skeleton of a small euornithopod in Porto das Barcas, Lourinhã.
The fossil was provisionally described in 2000 and nicknamed "Manuelino".
Fernando Escaso and colleagues formally named Eousdryosaurus in 2014, following a brief description in 2000.
Eousdryosaurus is based on the holotype SHN(JJS)-170, housed in the Sociedade de Historia Natural in Torres Vedras, Portugal.
A phylogenetic analysis by Escaso et al. placed Eousdryosaurus as a basal dryosaurid within the Dryomorpha, a group of small bipedal herbivores near the base of Iguanodontia.
Eousdryosaurus nanohallucis lived during the late Jurassic, approximately 152 million years ago, in what is now Europe.
The fossils were discovered in late Kimmeridgian-age sandstone (approximately 152 million years old) in the Lourinhã Formation, Portugal.
The time range for Eousdryosaurus is from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian (152.21 to 145.06 million years ago).
Dieudonné et al. (2020) suggested Eousdryosaurus is a sister taxon to the Elasmaria, contrasting with other studies.
The genus name references the animal being a relative of Dryosaurus located on the east side of the Atlantic Ocean.
The genus name references Eousdryosaurus being a relative of Dryosaurus that lived on the east side of the Atlantic Ocean.
Rotatori et al. (2024) found support for a dryosaurid position for Eousdryosaurus, contrasting with the suggestions of Dieudonné et al. (2020).
